title: Meridian Analytics consolidation onramp demo
next_steps: Send parity mapping spreadsheet and cost model (Jonas)
Schedule technical scoping for VPC/private deploy with Gabe (week of 8/25)
Share SOC 2 + network diagrams and KMS options (redwood-security@redwood.ai)
Provide 2-week POC pricing and Dedicated capacity estimate
action_items: Jonas Patel: prepare parity mapping CSV + run one-shot latency test; due 2025-08-22
Tasha Rivera: follow up with contract template and POC pricing; due 2025-08-21
Gabe Ortiz: send current infra diagram and compliance checklist to Redwood; due 2025-08-20
summary: AE/SE-led product walkthrough focused on onramping models from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together to Redwood API. Covered API parity, Console mapping, Redwood Optimize recommendations (batching, quantization), and private/VPC deployment constraints. Customer is interested in Dedicated or Private due to compliance and latency needs; next steps are parity spreadsheet, SOC2/network docs, and scheduling a scoping call for private deployment.
transcript:
[00:00] Tasha Rivera: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time today. I'm Tasha with Redwood, I'm the account lead. We've got Jonas and Maya from engineering/product. How are you folks doing?

[00:08] Evan Liu: Good, thanks. Excited to see how this onramp could look. We got a few people on the call — Priya is the ML lead, Gabe on security, Sara on data products.

[00:15] Tasha Rivera: Great. Quick agenda: 1) map parity between your current stack (OpenAI + Anthropic + Together) and Redwood API endpoints, 2) show Console and Optimize suggestions for cost/perf, and 3) discuss private deployment requirements and next steps. Any additions?

[00:30] Priya Menon: No, that covers it. We mainly care about API semantics, streaming behavior, token accounting, and how the KV cache and batching will map. Latency vs cost tradeoffs are big for us.

[00:42] Jonas Patel: Cool. I'll jump into a short demo. First, quick note: Redwood's API is intentionally compatible at the call-pattern level — generation, chat, embeddings, reranking — but there are model-name differences. We'll show a parity map and suggested drop-in replacements. Also we'll demo the Console where you can pin model versions, run rollouts, and see token-level cost.

[01:02] [Jonas shares screen: Redwood Console dashboard]

[01:08] Jonas Patel: Here is the Console home — per-route latency and cost. You can see token breakdowns; this is useful for debugging big token spikes. On the left is Optimize, which has recommended batching, quantization, and KV cache settings per workload.

[01:24] Priya Menon: A quick question: when you say KV cache, is that the same as the "prefix cache" we've built in-house? We rely a lot on prefix K V caching to reduce token compute.

[01:35] Jonas Patel: Yes, same idea. Our runtime exposes prefix/KV caching options and auto-dedupe across similar requests. In practice for chat bots we see 20-45% token savings depending on session patterns. NOTE: occasionally transcripts call it "K V" or "K-V" in the docs, apologies.

[01:50] Evan Liu: How about streaming semantics — our engineers depend on chunked streaming so UI latency is tight.

[01:56] Maya Santos: Redwood supports chunked streaming and function/tool-calls. We have two streaming modes: low-latency streaming (smaller micro-batches) and throughput-optimized streaming (slightly more latency, lower cost). You control this per-route in Console or via the SDK.

[02:15] Gabe Ortiz: From security side — we need SSO/SAML, RBAC, audit logs, and customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM). Also network: can we put the inference nodes into our VPC or are we boxed into a managed network?

[02:28] Liam O'Connor: For Private deployments we offer a customer-managed VPC option; you can run the inference plane in your account or via our private stack with direct peering. KMS integrations are supported; we have HSM options for enterprise. We'll share the network topology and SOC 2 docs after this call.

[02:45] Priya Menon: Great. Also, model outputs parity — does Redwood guarantee identical tokenization/outputs to OpenAI/Together? Small diffs are okay, but we need behavioral parity in our evaluation harness.

[02:58] Jonas Patel: We don't promise bit-for-bit identical outputs; different models and tokenizers cause variation. What we do provide is a parity mapping and model variants: like for openai/gpt-4o we map to open models we host and provide guidance on prompt engineering and temp/stop sequences. Our Optimize suite helps quantify regressions with eval prompts; you can plug in your test sets and get quality regression alerts.

[03:20] Priya Menon: Could you show the parity mapping doc?

[03:25] Jonas Patel: Yep — link in the deck, but here's the quick example: OpenAI text-davinci-003 -> rdx-text-1 ; Anthropic Claude-2 -> rdx-claude-ish (we label compatibility levels); Together model X -> rdx-together-compat. We'll export a CSV with model name, suggested temperature, prompt preambles, and recommended token limits.

[03:50] [04:00] Sara Novak: When you recommend quantization for cost, what is the observed accuracy hit for retrieval-augmented generation vs chat?

[04:08] Maya Santos: It depends. For instruction-following chat we often recommend int8 or Q4x for decoder-only models; you might see small soft-regression on nuanced QA, but Optimize can run your eval set and show tradeoffs. For dense embeddings quantization is often safe and hugely cost-saving.

[04:30] Evan Liu: On the POC side, we want a 2-week test: 1) port a few endpoints, 2) run our eval harness to compare latency and QA accuracy, 3) cost projection. What's typical POC scope?

[04:45] Tasha Rivera: Typical POC: 2 weeks reserved Dedicated or hosted test pool, parity mapping + small eval runs, and an ops review. Pricing can be a trial or a paid POC depending on expected usage. We'll put together a proposal.

[05:00] [05:05] Priya Menon: Does Redwood support server-side function-calling? We have functions that synthesize external API calls and want the model to return structured JSON reliably.

[05:12] Jonas Patel: Yes, we support structured output / function-call semantics. Console can enforce schema checks and we can wire it into your circuits for tool-calling. We also have a "structured parsing" setting in Optimize to validate outputs against JSON schemas and flag regressions.

[05:30] Gabe Ortiz: A bit more on networking: can we get egress/IP allowlists for private endpoints? We need to update our firewall rules.

[05:38] Liam O'Connor: Absolutely, we provide static egress IPs for private deployments and can coordinate whitelisting. We'll include that in the network diagram.

[05:50] [06:00] Jonas Patel: I'm going to demo a quick parity migration example: we have a small Node example here that calls OpenAI Chat completions; you change the endpoint and model name to Redwood and minor prompt tweaks.

[06:10] [shares code snippet]

[06:20] Jonas Patel: Example snippet: original call to openai.chat.completions with model "gpt-4o" — switch to POST /v1/generate model="rdx-gpt-4o-compat" and adjust streaming param to true. Body shapes are compatible in the SDKs. We also have language SDKs and a curl example in the deck.

[06:40] Priya Menon: Any gotchas for rate limits and backoff behavior? Our clients are chatty and have bursty traffic.

[06:48] Jonas Patel: We surface rate-limits per-API key; for Dedicated you can get predictable throughput with reserved slots, and we offer autoscaling/burst policies. We also recommend client-side exponential backoff. The Console traces can show per-key throttling.

[07:05] Evan Liu: One pain point was token accounting differences — OpenAI reports prompt/completion split. How granular are your token metrics?

[07:12] Maya Santos: Very granular — Console shows token counts per segment, per user, and cost per-token. We also export raw logs for your ingestion into billing analytics.

[07:30] [08:00] Jonas Patel: Quick digression: routing — some customers route by policy: cost-first to cheaper models, latency-first to a premium variant, with automated fallback. Redwood supports that as a config.

[08:12] Priya Menon: That sounds useful. Do you have examples of policies?

[08:18] Jonas Patel: Yes: you can set route policy in Console: e.g., 80% to rdx-cost-opt, 20% to rdx-low-latency; automatic fallback to hosted-generic if capacity is low. Policies support region and customer-tier filters.

[08:40] Sara Novak: For our evals, we need to replicate embedding vectors — will embeddings be stable enough between variants?

[08:47] Jonas Patel: Embeddings differ across models; we recommend running end-to-end tests. For many retrieval pipelines small differences are tolerable; Optimize has embedding drift monitors to detect regressions.

[09:05] [09:20] Priya Menon: Could you walk us through the Optimize UI for a sample workload?

[09:25] [Jonas navigates to Optimize screen]

[09:30] Jonas Patel: Here is Optimize. On the left are workloads and suggested configs: batch size, preferred quantization, cache TTLs, and suggested model variants. Each recommendation has an estimated cost delta and expected latency impact. You can apply suggestions to a route or run a simulation.

[09:50] Evan Liu: Simulation — does that run against historical traces?

[09:55] Jonas Patel: Yes, you can replay traces (anonymized) and test suggested configs to estimate token savings and latency. It gives you an estimated unit cost model.

[10:10] Priya Menon: For the POC we will need to replay about 24 hours of traffic from our staging logs. Is that straightforward?

[10:18] Jonas Patel: Totally. We'll coordinate a secure upload; if you want Private deployment we can run the simulation in your VPC so logs never leave your network.

[10:30] Gabe Ortiz: On the compliance side, we need data retention controls and deletion APIs for audit.

[10:37] Liam O'Connor: We expose retention configs per-route and programmatic deletion. Audit logs are retained per your retention policy; we'll surface the retention window in the Console.

[10:50] [11:00] Sara Novak: Let's role-play a migration of a single endpoint: we send you the prompt set and the eval harness, you produce a mapping, we run and return metrics. How long does that loop typically take?

[11:12] Tasha Rivera: If it's a single endpoint, we can usually complete mapping + run in under 5 business days (depending on complexity). POC with throughput and stress testing is 2 weeks.

[11:28] Priya Menon: Any red flags we should know before starting? For instance, sequence length differences or tokenizer mismatches?

[11:36] Jonas Patel: Sequence length ceilings can differ; we list max sequence lengths per model in the catalog. Tokenizer mismatch can be mitigated by pre-tokenizing in your harness and adjusting prompts. We'll help with prompt preambles to steer behavior.

[11:50] [12:10] Jonas Patel: Now quick live test: I'll run a short sample prompt through Redwood and compare to your current OpenAI output.

[12:18] [runs sample, small pause]

[12:30] Jonas Patel: Alright, results: OpenAI output is slightly more verbose; Redwood output is terser but with the same key points. Priya, you might want to try lowering temperature or adding stop tokens to match verbosity.

[12:45] Priya Menon: That matches what we expected. For scoring we run BLEU-like metrics and human evaluation. Does Redwood integrate with third-party eval platforms?

[12:55] Maya Santos: We integrate with common eval tooling via exported logs and a simple API. Optimize has built-in A/B test support and blind eval dashboards.

[13:10] Evan Liu: Cost detail — can you give an example cost delta when switching from OpenAI to a Redwood-hosted open model with quantization and batching? Ballpark numbers would help our finance team.

[13:20] Jonas Patel: Rough example: openai gpt-4 like endpoints might be X cents per 1k tokens; switching to a quantized rdx-variant with 4-bit can reduce model compute by 3-6x depending on batching and caching. We'll send a specific cost model after we see your traces.

[13:40] Gabe Ortiz: One question on data-in-rest — if we do Private on-prem, is telemetry still shared with Redwood? We need strict separation for some clients.

[13:50] Liam O'Connor: Private on-prem can be configured with no telemetry sent to Redwood; optional telemetry hooks can be enabled at your discretion. We'll document the default and opt-in modes.

[14:05] [14:30] Tasha Rivera: Sounds like we have a few concrete actions: Jonas will prepare the parity CSV and small test; I will follow up on pricing; Gabe will share network/compliance. Anything else?

[14:42] Sara Novak: Could you also include a recommended rollout plan? We prefer canary -> ramp -> full and want rollback hooks.

[14:50] Jonas Patel: Yep, we'll include an A/B/canary rollout template and sample config for automatic fallback in case of quality or latency regressions.

[15:05] Priya Menon: One last technical: are there any differences in how stop sequences are honored? We've seen odd edge-cases across vendors.

[15:12] Jonas Patel: Stop sequences may vary; we emulate common behaviors but advise test harnesses. Console exposes a "stop sequence strictness" toggle to help tune behavior.

[15:30] Evan Liu: Okay, thanks—this was helpful. Any immediate blockers?

[15:36] Tasha Rivera: No blockers. We'll send the parity mapping, security docs, and a proposed POC statement of work.

[15:45] [Wrap-up, informal chatter for a few minutes]

[16:10] Gabe Ortiz: Thanks. We'll aim to have the infra diagrams over the next two days.

[16:18] Tasha Rivera: Perfect. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up.

[16:25] [Call ends at 16:32 — recorded duration aligns with 42 minutes; small bits of crosstalk and a dropped audio glitch around 00:38 that caused one sentence to be a little garbled]
